rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient to retain weakly retained compounds while promoting elution of all 10 compounds within the acquisition window. The retention and resolution pattern will guide subsequent optimization of gradient range, duration, and temperature.

Halve the gradient duration to reduce the time penalty while testing whether the current resolution margin is sufficient. Keep temperature and gradient endpoints fixed to isolate the effect of gradient steepness.

Test whether higher temperature separates the crowded middle peaks while preserving the short run's zero time penalty. Holding the gradient fixed isolates temperature-dependent changes in selectivity.

The temperature increase resolved the original crowded region but introduced a different near-coelution. Testing 55 °C may separate that new critical pair while retaining adequate resolution elsewhere and a zero time penalty.

A slightly shallower gradient may resolve the near-coelution seen at 60 °C while preserving separation of the other middle peaks. The last peak should still elute early enough to avoid a time penalty.

Combine the better selectivity at 55 °C with the shallower 12-minute gradient to improve the remaining critical pair. The projected last-peak time is approximately 7.6 minutes, likely retaining a zero time penalty.

Test a slightly shallower gradient near the maximum-scoring method to increase separation of the first critical pair while checking that the second remains resolved. The last peak is expected near 8 minutes, potentially preserving the zero time penalty.

The maximum CRF is already achieved; test a higher starting organic fraction as an alternative that may shorten retention while maintaining full resolution. This probes initial-composition sensitivity around the best method.

Slightly reduce gradient steepness to improve the R = 1.29 critical pair from injection 8 while retaining the other pair's resolution margin. This may provide another maximum-scoring method with all peaks eluting before 8 minutes.

A further small decrease in gradient steepness should raise the R = 1.47 critical pair above 1.5 while preserving the other pair's margin. The last peak is projected near 8 minutes, testing whether this alternative can also achieve CRF 1.000.

This gradient slope lies between injections 9 and 10, potentially balancing both critical resolutions above 1.5 with the last peak just under 8 minutes. The maximum CRF is already attained; this tests an alternative with slightly more time margin than injection 10.

With the maximum score already secured, test a lower-temperature selectivity regime for an alternative fast method. Cooling may separate the crowded middle peaks seen at 40 °C, though the earlier close pair and last-peak time require checking.

Probe temperature sensitivity 5 °C below the maximum-scoring method. This should improve the earlier critical pair but may compress the later pair, establishing how strongly full resolution depends on maintaining 55 °C.

Test a faster, higher-organic start at 60 °C to move away from the near-coelution observed with the longer gradients at that temperature. This explores a distinct short-run selectivity regime while retaining the established CRF 1.000 methods as the campaign best.

Increase the starting organic fraction one step to test whether the remaining close pair at 60 °C separates further while the neighboring pairs remain resolved. This explores a faster alternative to the established maximum-scoring methods.

Test whether a higher starting organic fraction improves the remaining close pair, with a longer gradient to protect neighboring separations. This explores another fast-method compromise; the previously achieved CRF of 1.000 remains the maximum possible score.

Return to the successful 55 °C selectivity regime and pair a higher starting organic fraction with a shallower gradient. This may provide another fully resolved method near the zero-time-penalty boundary, with improved resolution margin for the later critical pair.

Preserve injection 6's gradient slope and temperature while ending the gradient at a lower organic fraction. Since its last peak eluted before this shortened gradient would finish at the outlet, this method should retain CRF 1.000 while reducing organic solvent use during the subsequent hold.

Preserve injection 10's gradient slope and temperature while lowering the final organic fraction. The gradient ends at the outlet at 8.65 minutes, after the previously observed last peak, so this should retain its maximum CRF and minimum resolution of 1.58.

Keep the maximum-scoring gradient slope but begin the final hold earlier, after the first nine peaks have eluted. This tests whether 50% organic can elute the last compound without a time penalty while preserving the critical separations.

Slightly flatten injection 10's gradient to improve its earlier critical pair while checking that the later pair remains above 1.5. The projected last-peak time is about 8.45 minutes, potentially retaining zero time penalty given injection 20's result.

Test a gradient slope between injections 10 and 21, where both critical pairs should remain resolved. The last peak is expected near 8.2 minutes, giving another likely maximum-scoring method with more time margin than injection 21.

Test a shallower gradient with a lower final organic fraction to extend the mapped range of fully resolved methods. The critical resolutions are projected to remain above 1.5, but the last peak may begin to incur a time penalty; the established maximum-scoring methods remain preferred if so.

Use injection 9's gradient slope but transition to the final hold before the last compound elutes, testing a lower-organic alternative. The earlier critical pair is expected to remain marginal, so this primarily checks the effect of the hold while preserving the established maximum-scoring methods.

Finish with a gradient slope between the maximum-scoring injections 21 and 22, predicting full resolution and a last-peak time near 8.3 minutes. This tests another likely CRF 1.000 method; the campaign has already attained the highest possible score.
